criteria_quotes: No proprietary Arkansas Medicaid (Fee-for-Service) medical policy document containing specific medical-necessity criteria for CPT code 63030 is publicly available. However, Arkansas Medicaid's prior authorization reviews are performed by the Arkansas Foundation for Medical Care (AFMC), which utilizes established national clinical screening guidelines (such as InterQual or MCG) combined with professional judgment. Standard InterQual screening criteria for CPT 63030 (Lumbar discectomy/decompression) typically require:
1. Nerve root compression by imaging [One]: MRI, CT, or MYL-CT
2. Symptoms/findings of unilateral radiculopathy with motor deficit or sensory deficit (pain, paresthesias, or numbness in a nerve root distribution)

3. Failure of conservative treatment [Both]: A) NSAIDs or other anti-inflammatories (unless contraindicated) for >= 3 weeks, AND B) Activity modification (provocative activity limitation or physical therapy) for >= 6 weeks
4. Exception to conservative therapy: Urgent surgery is indicated for progressive motor weakness or cauda equina syndrome (bowel/bladder dysfunction or saddle anesthesia).

answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: The patient can obtain the exact clinical criteria applied to their determination by contacting the Arkansas Department of Human Services (DHS) Division of Medical Services or their review vendor, the Arkansas Foundation for Medical Care (AFMC). Under the Arkansas Prior Authorization Transparency Act (Ark. Code § 23-99-1104), utilization review entities are legally required to disclose all prior authorization requirements, restrictions, and written clinical criteria.
answer.notes: Standard Arkansas Medicaid (Fee-for-Service) delegates utilization review and prior authorization to the Arkansas Foundation for Medical Care (AFMC). While individual managed care options (such as Arkansas Total Care or Summit Community Care PASSE plans) publish their reliance on InterQual and MCG clinical criteria, standard FFS Medicaid does not publish a standalone, branded clinical policy for CPT 63030. To appeal, the member must submit a written request for a Fair Hearing (using Form DHS-1200 or a custom letter) to the DHS Appeals and Hearings Section. Although standard state regulations often require fair hearing requests within 30 to 35 calendar days, the patient's specific denial notice explicitly grants them 180 days (until 2027-01-30) to submit their appeal.

Decompressive surgery for disc disease does not generally result in instability so accompanying fusion is not often necessary. Satisfactory results can be achieved with disc surgery alone. Because better long-term results have not been seen with discectomy performed with fusion and because this surgery has the potential for serious complications, requests for spinal fusion with hemilaminectomy require secondary medical review. (3)-RIN: For criteria covering microdiscectomy or percutaneous lumbar discectomy, see the "Discectomy, Lumbar" criteria subset. (4) While degenerative changes may be present at multiple levels, nerve root compression typically presents at only one or two levels. Surgery is appropriate at the levels of nerve root compression and not as prophylaxis at other levels without compression. Foraminotomy (surgery on the intervertebral foramen) may be indicated as an adjunct to hemilaminectomy if the nerve root compression is secondary to narrowing of the foramen. (5)-DEF: Foraminal stenosis is a degenerative condition resulting in narrowing of the foramina and compression of a nerve root. (6) In the lumbar spine, the ruptured disc generally compresses the root at the level below the disc rupture (e.g., a ruptured disc at level L2-L3 compresses the L3 root). Infrequently, a ruptured disc impinges far enough vertically or horizontally to compress the root at the level above the rupture. (7) Disc bulging and degeneration are common imaging findings in patients without symptoms or PE findings. These criteria address disc pathology seen by imaging which causes neurocompression. (8) Compression usually affects the sensory neurons of the nerve root first, causing pain and paresthesias. Motor neurons are somewhat less vulnerable, and are usually affected later or in more severe compression. Neurologic findings of sensory loss and reflex loss are corroborative findings for compressive radiculopathy but are not substitutes for radicular pain or muscle weakness. (9)-DEF: Radiculopathy refers to sensory or motor dysfunction in the discrete distribution of an involved nerve root. (10)-MDR: Severe atrophy indicates long-standing disease that may not be amenable to surgical correction. Requests for surgery in these cases require secondary medical review. (11) Muscle strength can be graded on a 0 to 5 scale (0 is no visible or palpable muscle contraction and 5 is normal strength) (Braddom and Buschbacher, Physical medicine and rehabilitation, 2nd ed. 2000). For the purposes of these criteria, severe muscle weakness is defined as "less than 2 out of 5" muscle strength by PE (less than full ROM with gravity eliminated) or the inability to ambulate. It is a matter of local medical policy whether to accept acetaminophen or other analgesics as alternatives for NSAIDs. (14) Contraindications to NSAIDs may be absolute (e.g., pregnancy, history of allergic reaction) or relative (e.g., anticoagulant use, history of PUD). (15) Activity modification for lumbar radiculopathy involves limiting activities that provoke or aggravate symptoms, such as heavy lifting, repetitive bending, or prolonged standing. PT with exercises to improve posture and strengthen the lumbar muscles may be beneficial in some patients. (16) Urgent surgery should be considered for patients with progressive motor weakness. (17)-MDR: Back pain without radicular pain is not an indication for decompressive surgery. These cases require secondary medical review. (18) Pain in radiculopathy is present in a specific nerve root distribution: • Hip, thigh, and knee pain (L3) • Hip, thigh, knee, and medial leg pain (L4) • Hip, lateral thigh, and leg pain (L5) • Buttock, posterior thigh, and calf pain (S1) Anatomic variation can exist in these nerve root distributions. Early on in the disease process the entire nerve root distribution may not be affected. (19) Epidural steroid injections are a treatment option for patients with continued radicular pain following failure of noninvasive treatment. Although their effectiveness is debated, a trial of steroid injections may be considered for the patient who wants to avoid surgery. Randomized, controlled trials on the efficacy of epidural injections show mixed results with only a few studies reporting improvement with injection as compared with control. Results from other less rigorous studies are difficult to evaluate due to variation in study design, patient selection, injection techniques, and length of patient follow-up. Rates of patient improvement have been reported from 0% to 75% with the use of epidural injection (Fanciullo et al., Reg Anesth Pain Med 2001; 26(1): 5-11). Simultaneous rupture at more than two levels with concomitant radiculopathy is uncommon. (21) Spinal nerve roots and compression are associated with a specific spinal column level. Compression of the L3 nerve root usually occurs at the L2-L3 level; L4 compression at L3-L4; L5 compression at L4-L5; and S1 compression usually occurs at the L5-S1 level.
